extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students of narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on handling point of view and the dramatization of consciousness in the novel—how to present a character's inner life, when to withhold authorial knowledge, and how to make pictorial or undramatic subjects act like drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach the subject through the character's consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: “the subject can only be reached through Strether’s consciousness... That way alone will command the impression that the scene makes on him. Nothing in the scene has any importance, any value in itself; what Strether sees in it—that is the whole of its meaning.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present scenes only insofar as they are perceived and given meaning by the focal character; the reader's impression should be mediated by that character's sensory and mental reception rather than by an objective catalogue of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize thought by showing its surface images
rubrics_metrics.description: “the author must so arrange matters that Strether’s thought will all be made intelligible by a direct view of its surface... The immediate flaw or ripple of the moment, and the next and the next, will then take up the tale, like the speakers in a dialogue.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent inner life as a sequence of observable images, gestures, pauses and small mental movements rather than by abstract exposition; let the surface manifestations of thought enact the inner process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from authorial intrusion and authoritative telling
rubrics_metrics.description: “Henry James knows all there is to-know of Strether, but he most carefully refrains — from using his knowledge. He wishes us to accept nothing from him, on authority—only to watch and learn.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stepping in as an omniscient commentator who supplies conclusions; withhold authorial summaries so readers must build understanding from presented action and impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid retrospective exposition where demonstration is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: “A mere account of its working, after the fact, has already been barred; we have found that this of necessity is lacking in force, it is statement where we look for demonstration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute narrated summaries for enacted scenes when the aim is to show how a mind or situation changes; exposition frequently weakens the dramatic effect and misleads if it replaces demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controlled shifts of point of view to inform the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: “there is in fact an insidious shifting of it, so artfully contrived that the reader may arrive at the end without suspecting the trick... the reader, all unawares, is placed in a better position for an understanding of Strether’s history, better than the position of Strether himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtle, artful shifts of focalization can place the reader slightly 'ahead' or more informed than the focal character, enhancing irony or insight—do this with care so it feels natural and does not betray the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat scenes dramati cally to make characters appear objective
rubrics_metrics.description: “Simply it consists in treating the scene as dramatically as possible—keeping it framed in Strether’s vision, certainly, but keeping his consciousness out of sight, his thought unexplored.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character takes part in dialogue or action, you may present them as if observed from outside (their voice belonging to someone we watch) by refraining from interior exposition during the scene; this grants them an almost independent, objective presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let a first-person/autobiographical narrator undercut dramatic immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “If Strether were really the narrator... he could not hold back, he could not heighten the story of his thought with that touch of suspense... His narration must have discounted the effect of his outburst.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using first-person or autobiographical frameworks where sudden, surprising dramatic action is needed—such narrators will tend to explain and thereby weaken immediacy and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert pictorial/undramatic subjects into drama by method
rubrics_metrics.description: “The less dramatic, strictly speaking, the subject may be... the more it is needful to heighten its flat, pictorial, descriptive surface by the arts of drama... It animates the actual elements of the picture, the description, and makes a drama of these.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For subjects that are essentially states or conditions rather than actions, use dramatic techniques (scene, gesture, focused images) to animate descriptions instead of padding with irrelevant dialogue or expository lumps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal hidden facts indirectly—surround rather than state them
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not to walk straight up to the fact and put it into phrases, but to surround the fact, and so to detach it inviolate... The glimpse, so rendered, tells nothing. But ... we have seen Milly when she believed herself unseen, and it is certain that there is more in her mind than now appears.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let crucial truths emerge by implication, small signs, and selective glimpses; do not state central facts in blunt prose when indirect revelation produces stronger, more substantial effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build solidity of impression stereoscopically
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some method which will enable an onlooker to see round the object, to left and right, as far as possible, just as with two eyes, stereoscopically, we shape and solidify the flat impression of a sphere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accumulate multiple peripheral observations and viewpoints so that an inner state or character grows three-dimensional in the reader's mind; use varied small moments rather than a single authoritative account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gestures, looks and small particulars to externalize thought
rubrics_metrics.description: “The story that is concerned... with the impact of experience upon a mind... thought has its tell-tale gestures and its speaking looks, just as much as an actor on the stage. Make use of these looks and gestures, express the story through them, leave them to enact it—”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make interior life visible through physical, behavioral, and expressive detail; rely on these external signs to show what characters think and feel instead of explicit interior narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit a narrator when they add no specific value
rubrics_metrics.description: “I take it as evident that unless the presence of a seer and a recorder is made a value in itself, contributing definitely to the effect of the subject, he is better dispensed with and put out of the way; where other things are equal a direct view of the matter in hand is the best.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply narrative economy: only retain an explicit narrator if their perspective or commentary materially contributes to the effect; otherwise present events directly so readers can form impressions themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve mystery by excluding the mind of the central knower
rubrics_metrics.description: “In a tale of murder and mystery there is one man who cannot possibly be the narrator, and that is the murderer himself; for if he admits us into his mind at all he must do so without reserve, thereby betraying the secret that we ought to be guessing at for ourselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving privileged interior access to characters who, if fully disclosed, would dissolve the suspense or mystery essential to the plot; withhold perspectives that would prematurely reveal key secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes to replace 'harking back to make up' narrative lumps
rubrics_metrics.description: “he himself... calls attention to the way in which a conversation between Strether and Maria Gostrey... puts the reader in possession of all the past facts of the situation which it is necessary for him to know; a scene thus takes the place of that ‘harking back to make up,’ ... which is apt to appear as a lump of narrative.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey necessary backstory by embedding it within scenes and dialogue rather than through large blocks of retrospective summary; let scenes organically supply required context.
